report:
## Conclusion

Your view is supported: **there is no reliable clinical evidence that soursop (also called graviola or *Annona muricata*) cures cancer in humans.** Claims that it does are false.

### Why the claim persists
Soursop contains compounds called acetogenins. Extracts and isolated compounds have shown cancer-cell toxicity in laboratory experiments, and some animal research has been reported. But killing cells in a dish—or affecting tumors in animals—does not establish that a food, tea, or supplement safely treats cancer in people. It does not determine an effective human dose, whether the compound reaches a tumor, or whether harms outweigh benefits.

### What human evidence shows
A review of the human literature found only limited evidence and concluded that the absence of high-quality studies makes it impossible to draw conclusions about anticancer effectiveness. Cancer Research UK likewise says there is not enough reliable evidence that graviola works as a cancer treatment, and that reputable cancer organizations do not support cure claims.

### Safety and practical implications
“Natural” does not mean proven or harmless. Concentrated leaf/extract supplements are materially different from eating the fruit as food; product contents and doses can vary. Most importantly, substituting soursop for evidence-based cancer care can delay treatments known to improve survival. Discuss any supplement or herbal tea with the oncology team, especially because of possible adverse effects and treatment interactions.

Soursop can be eaten as a fruit if appropriate for someone’s diet, but it should **not** be presented or used as a cancer cure.
